data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"A panel of trained non-experts using an explicit checklist will produce more reliable judgments than a single expert using intuition for objectively verifiable tasks, provided the checklist decomposes the evaluation into independent sub-criteria whose joint presence is causally necessary for the correct outcome.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the checklist items are merely correlated with the correct answer but not causally necessary, panelists might score high on compliance while failing on novel or edge cases.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the task requires recognizing emergent gestalt properties not decomposable into independent items, the non-expert panel will consistently fail where an expert's intuition succeeds.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If panelists' judgments on checklist items are not independent (e.g., shared cultural biases), the error-reduction benefit of aggregation collapses.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The checklist enforces a decomposition of the task into component judgments. Individual non-experts can recognize surface features corresponding to these sub-criteria. When aggregated, the panel averages out individual perceptual errors. This works only if the objective correctness of the outcome depends on a conjunctive (necessary) set of features the checklist captures.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
